Avarice
ăv´a-rĭs
n. (an inordinate desire of gain; greediness after wealth)
Latin avaritia, from avere, to crave. The older English distinguishes avarice, the craving to get, from covetousness, the craving for what is another's; Scripture treats them as one disease.

Biblical Definition

Avarice is the inordinate desire of gain, and the Lord warns against it in a way that anticipates every defence: “Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15). Paul names it a root: “the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows” (1Ti 6:10). He classes it with idolatry: “covetousness, which is idolatry” (Col 3:5). Proverbs names the end: “so are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof” (Pro 1:19). And the Preacher names the mechanism: “He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver” (Ecc 5:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines avarice as an inordinate desire of gaining and possessing wealth; covetousness; greediness or insatiable desire of gain.

expand to see more

AVARICE, n. An inordinate desire of gaining and possessing wealth; covetousness; greediness or insatiable desire of gain.

Avarice is the vice of declining years.

2. An inordinate desire of other things; as an avarice of praise.

AVARICIOUS, a. Covetous; greedy of gain; immoderately desirous of accumulating property.

Key Scripture

Luk 12:15 — "And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth."

1Ti 6:10 — "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows."

Col 3:5 — "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:"

Pro 1:19 — "So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof."

Ecc 5:10 — "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity."

Modern Corruption

Avarice is the one sin nobody confesses, because it is always the next man who has too much.

expand to see more

Every other sin has a threshold a man can admit he has crossed. Avarice does not, because the standard is always set just above one's own holdings; the greedy man is the one with more, and the man with less is prudent rather than poor. This is why the Lord prefaces His warning with take heed, and beware — a doubled caution He does not attach to adultery or theft. The sin hides inside ordinary financial competence, and a congregation will discipline a drunkard for years before it notices a covetous elder.

Colossians 3:5 supplies the diagnosis that explains the persistence: covetousness which is idolatry. It is not merely that money can be loved too much; it is that money offers what God offers — security, standing, freedom, a future — and does so without requiring faith. That is why 1 Timothy 6:10 says those who coveted after it have erred from the faith, since a man who has secured his soul elsewhere no longer needs the promises. The piercing with many sorrows comes afterwards, when the security proves to be exactly as durable as a currency.

Ecclesiastes 5:10 states the trap in the plainest form available: he that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver. The appetite is structurally incapable of being met by its object, so more of the object cannot cure it. Every generation rediscovers this and none acts on it. The remedy Scripture gives is not a lower income but a different set of affections — contentment, which Paul says he learned (Php 4:11), and generosity, which is avarice run in reverse and is the only spending that reliably weakens the love of money.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek pleonexia (G4124), covetousness, a desire for more; philarguria (G5365), love of money; Hebrew betsa (H1215), unjust gain; ahab keseph (H157, H3701), to love silver.

expand to see more

Greek pleonexia (G4124) — literally the desire for more; Luke 12:15, Colossians 3:5, Ephesians 5:3, Mark 7:22.

Greek philarguria (G5365) — love of money; 1 Timothy 6:10 only; the adjective philarguros, Luke 16:14, 2 Timothy 3:2.

Hebrew betsa (H1215) — gain, unjust profit; Proverbs 1:19, 28:16, Exodus 18:21, Jeremiah 6:13.

Usage

"“Take heed, and beware” — a doubled caution, attached to this sin."

"“Covetousness, which is idolatry” — because it offers what God offers."

"“He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver” — more cannot cure it."
